summary:
Curaçao stands under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here. It is an autonomous constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, holding full autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and matters reserved to the Supreme Court of the Netherlands.

In April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed that LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should receive equal rights without delay, and a package of rights requests was delivered to ministers in The Hague. Curaçao's commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano publicly endorsed equal rights for everyone.

That endorsement ran against organised opposition from within her own party. Winifred Raveneau's fierce resistance had already forced Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel after a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement, and parliamentary opposition to equal-rights measures continued even as the island's own government publicly backed the community.

Community infrastructure exists but is small. An LGBT centre, the Pink House, opened in Curaçao in 2010, and reporting from GlobalGayz (updated January 2017) treats Curaçao, Aruba and Bonaire as quietly gay-friendly places within the Kingdom while crediting Curaçao, with Sint Maarten and Aruba, as a driver of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom. Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag cites an IGLTA award naming the island the most gay-welcoming in the region.

For a trans visitor the composite reads as low legal risk with thin trans-specific infrastructure: no documented state hostility toward trans people, an active but negotiating community, and no sourced local gender-recognition pathway or trans-specific care capacity.
tangentialFactors:
Aruba, Curaçao's fellow constituent country in the Kingdom, passed same-sex civil partnerships on 8 September 2016. That is comparator context for the direction of Kingdom policy, not Curaçao law, and it does not establish partner recognition on Curaçao itself.

Regional travel-culture surveys place the ABC islands — Aruba, Bonaire and Curaçao — in a quiet, tolerant mainstream, a framing that describes general gay-friendliness rather than any trans-specific guarantee.

The record shows a persistent gap between Kingdom-level intent and island-level practice: an equal-rights agreement signed by all Kingdom governments in 2015 sits alongside a 2013 Pride permit issued on such short notice and under such strict conditions that the event had to move venue. Because Curaçao governs its own internal affairs, the permitting authority a visitor's event would face is local.
localsOnly:
Residents have had an LGBT community centre, the Pink House, since 2010, and Curaçao is described in Kingdom-level reporting as one of the constituent countries driving equal-rights moves alongside Sint Maarten and Aruba.

Domestic politics is split on the question. Commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano publicly backed equal rights for everyone in 2015, while her party colleague Winifred Raveneau mounted fierce opposition and used the permit process to obstruct the 2013 Gay Pride. Residents therefore live with official support and organised parliamentary resistance at the same time.

Advocacy has been routed through the Kingdom's central government: a rights wishes-package was delivered to ministers in The Hague after the 2015 agreement among Kingdom governments' representatives.

Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag points to an IGLTA award naming the island the most gay-welcoming in the region as evidence of its standing.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses a gender-recognition pathway for trans people in Curaçao: whether a legal procedure exists, what it requires, or which authority decides is unresolved here.

Entry, visa and border-screening practices that could expose a visitor's trans status are not sourced, nor are document or marker rules for passports and identity papers issued in Curaçao or by the Netherlands.

Hate-crime or hate-speech protection covering gender identity, and any enforcement record under it, is not sourced. Nor is trans-specific healthcare capacity, its availability to visitors, or any exclusion of trans-related care.

Whether the Pride permit friction documented in 2013 recurred after that year, and whether the 2015 Kingdom equal-rights agreement has been implemented in Curaçao legislation, both remain unresolved on this inventory.

No sub-national variation within Curaçao is sourced; the island is treated as a single unit throughout.
